title: Anthropic’s unusual IPO process chafes some bankers
html:
The Anthropic logo on the Nasdaq MarketSite tower in New York on Thursday.Andres Kudacki/The Associated Press

For the second time this year, Wall Street bankers and lawyers took home a massive paycheque from a record-setting initial public offering. And for the second time this year, some of them came out of it complaining in private about how the process was riddled with complications and unlike any they had worked on before.

With SpaceX’s IPO in June, in which banks earned half a billion dollars in fees, bankers chafed over how tightly the Elon Musk-led company controlled the months-long process and kept financial and other information private, making it hard for advisers to do their jobs.

As Anthropic’s ANTW-A IPO, dubbed internally “Project Lantern,” eclipsed SpaceX on Thursday and bankers took home more than half a billion dollars in fees, several people close to the process listed a litany of problems that had plagued the offering process: a compressed timeline, marred by last-minute changes and delays in sharing financial projections; rushed document approvals; and highly unusual restrictions on bankers and concern about leaks – especially after Reuters reported many details from a draft IPO filing weeks before it was made public.

Anthropic, for example, instructed some of its 22 IPO underwriters to limit the number of bankers working on the deal to four, asking the firms to make sure they were senior staff, several people familiar with the matter said. One of the people said the restriction likely came out of fear that information would leak, and that the banks found a way to work around it anyway.

Underlying these complaints is a new power dynamic between technology companies and Wall Street. Companies such as SpaceX, Anthropic – and potentially also OpenAI in the future – have come to wield enormous power as the transformative potential of artificial intelligence creates a frenzied demand for their shares, and they are wielding it to do things their way. That is upsetting some bankers. But banks and investors appear to have little choice but to play along.

“These companies certainly did have some market power to tell underwriters that it’s not going to be business as usual,” said Jay Ritter, a University of Florida professor emeritus who researches IPOs. “But the big Wall Street firms, I suspect, are still going to be doing things as business as usual for all but maybe OpenAI (after these two deals).”

Ritter added that both SpaceX and Anthropic had negotiated to pay underwriters nothing on the additional shares sold through the greenshoe option. “I don’t think most companies are going to be able to demand zero spread on overallotment shares,” he said.

Anthropic, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, the two lead underwriters on the two IPOs, declined to comment.

SpaceX and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment.

Both SpaceX and Anthropic debuted successfully, raising record amounts of money, and their shares rallied initially. A key part of the underwriters’ job is to market the securities. Thanks to the demand for AI, that was an easy sell – both companies had order books oversubscribed many times over.

After an initial burst in shares, the trajectories of the two big AI firms diverged. SpaceX climbed to a post-listing peak of US$201.80 on June 16 before retreating below its US$135 IPO price for the first time in mid-July. Anthropic’s shares closed down 8.5 per cent on Friday after a 17 per cent first-day pop, as a dramatic unravelling of the AI trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector.

In the case of SpaceX’s IPO, the people close to the process said Musk’s team dictated terms at every stage. Musk’s team told the largest and most powerful US banks – including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley – how to market SpaceX’s stock and to whom. It told some banks the specific order sizes they needed to “fill” – in some cases a few billion dollars – and gave them instructions on what types of investors to bring. Banks signed on to underwrite the IPO without being told what they would be paid, the people said.

The underlying current running through Anthropic’s IPO process was what several of the people who spoke to Reuters interpreted as a sense of extreme caution.

Anthropic asked some senior officers at banks working on its IPO to sign legal documents restricting core members of the transaction team from working with rival companies, including OpenAI, Cursor, DeepSeek and Hugging Face, for six months after it went public, according to the people.

Banks routinely manage conflicts and protect client confidentiality. But bankers and lawyers said it is rare for an IPO to impose exclusivity this broad, particularly on individual bankers.

In previous head-to-head IPOs such as those of ridesharing rivals Uber and Lyft, or real estate companies Trulia and Zillow, banks could simply pick a side, in part because the deals were smaller and required fewer banks.

Anthropic, by contrast, needed a broad syndicate to raise the enormous amount of capital it was seeking. That, some of the people said, explained why Anthropic sought to bind individual bankers with these restrictions.

One banker who declined to sign on to the agreement said it was a challenge to find people who could promise not to actively cover or engage with Anthropic’s peers, especially as several of those companies pursue their own initial or secondary offerings.

Some of the restrictions were meant to control leaks of information.

Nearly four weeks before Anthropic’s filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, called Form S-1, was made public, Reuters reported on it, revealing details of the company’s financials, risk factors, dealings with other tech companies and other information.

Anthropic also used a product called NetRoadshow to share information, instead of regular PDFs, with most of the banks underwriting the deal.

NetRoadshow logs access details, including information such as who has seen the document and looked at which page. Documents on NetRoadshow also had individual bankers’ names as watermarks.

Leaks continued to surface in the press, but using NetRoadshow complicated bankers’ work, including because the platform would not let them save copies of documents, one of the people said.

Anthropic planned to file an updated securities filing, called an S-1A, with the SEC with the price range and to launch the marketing on Nov. 10. To do so, it needed to send a draft to all the banks in its syndicate for them to sign off on it.

The night before it was to happen, a law firm on the deal sent a PDF to the banks about the sale of shares in Canada. But soon it followed with another e-mail asking them to disregard it, saying it “contains incorrect price range and share information,” according to the email, which was seen by Reuters.

The correct S-1A was then sent via the NetRoadshow platform around 2 a.m. New York time. Banks were told they had several hours to sign off on it before it was filed with the SEC.

The Globe and Mail is part of a coalition of news publishers that is suing Anthropic in Ontario court for unauthorized use of copyrighted materials.
summary: Compressed timeline and rushed document approvals among litany of issues that plagued offering process
